medical.title: Less intraoperative crystalloid fluid not tied to worse surgical outcomes
medical.summary: Substantially reduced intraoperative crystalloid fluid administration is not associated with worse patient-centered surgical outcomes, according to a study published online Sept. 15 in JAMA Network Open.

medical.title: Peptide may offer multipronged approach to neurodegenerative disease
medical.summary: Alzheimer's disease and related neurodegenerative disorders are among medicine's most challenging conditions, progressively impairing memory, movement and independence. Now, researchers at the University of California San Diego School of Medicine have identified a naturally occurring peptide—a small protein fragment called catestatin (CST)—that may help counter several key processes driving neurodegeneration.

medical.title: Same depression diagnosis, opposite brain patterns: Five profiles emerge
medical.summary: According to the World Health Organization, depression affects roughly 332 million (5.2%) adults globally. In Finland, depression is the most common single cause of both prolonged absences due to illness and disability pensions. Because two people with considerably different symptoms may receive the same depression diagnosis, researchers at the University of Helsinki wanted to determine whether this individuality also appears in brain activity.

medical.title: How a specific protein may drive brain damage in neuroHIV
medical.summary: While powerful medications can suppress the spread of HIV and its progression to AIDS, there are no cures, and many people living with HIV experience nervous system problems. Called neuroHIV, these complications occur when HIV infection affects the function and structural integrity of the brain and, to some extent, the spinal cord and peripheral nervous system.

medical.title: Teen mental health problems rise, with sharper increase among girls than boys
medical.summary: In the first survey period (2007–2008), around 10% of girls were above the threshold for clinically significant mental health problems. In the second survey period (2024–2025), the corresponding figure was about 30%—approximately three times higher.

medical.title: What science says about ultraprocessed foods and the aging brain
medical.summary: The colorings, additives and preservatives added to food products, as well as food processing techniques, are a source of concern in 2026 because they are ubiquitous worldwide, yet their effects on metabolic health are not fully understood. Researchers are also increasingly investigating how they may affect the brain as people age. Dr. Owen Carmichael of LSU's Pennington Biomedical Research Center is helping advance that understanding through a comprehensive look at the potential relationship between ultraprocessed foods—those featuring extensive processing and additives—and the aging brain.

medical.title: Blood tests could identify early signs of cancer years before diagnosis
medical.summary: A study of blood samples collected up to nine years before a cancer diagnosis found changes in the DNA that captured the body's response to early traces of cancer development.

medical.title: New filters help genetic sequencing flag possible causes of meningitis and encephalitis
medical.summary: New research led by Aston University's Dr. Ghaniah Hassan-Smith has found a new way to diagnose infections of the central nervous system, such as meningitis and encephalitis, that can be difficult to identify using conventional methods.

medical.title: Should you get a prostate-specific antigen test for prostate cancer?
medical.summary: Prostate cancer is common. About 200 in every 1,000 Australian men will be told they have prostate cancer by age 85. But the chance of dying from it is much lower: around 18 in 1,000 cases.

medical.title: Dementia caregiving can expose hidden family tensions—but early planning can ease the strain
medical.summary: "Families are messy, aren't they?" a daughter commented during a series of focus groups I ran with caregivers of older adults with memory issues.

medical.title: Social media offers little substitute for real-life emotional support, research suggests
medical.summary: Two new papers by Oregon State University scientists suggest that social media may do little to replace the emotional support people receive from in-person relationships and that the timing of social media use may matter for a person's mental health.

medical.title: Turning scar-forming cells into neurons helps restore movement after spinal cord injury
medical.summary: What if cells that form scars after a spinal cord injury could become part of the repair process? Researchers have developed a genetic system that converts certain scar-forming cells into neurons, improving movement in mice and rats with spinal cord injuries.

medical.title: Fiber is both diet fad and fixture for good health—why there is no one‑size‑fits‑all way to increase intake
medical.summary: The numbers are clear: Americans aren't getting enough fiber.

medical.title: 'Frustration brake failure' hypothesis proposes new way to understand addiction
medical.summary: Why does a person continue seeking drugs when doing so becomes increasingly difficult, frustrating or harmful? Researchers at The University of Texas Medical Branch (UTMB) propose that part of the answer may involve a breakdown in a natural behavioral "brake" that normally signals when it is time to stop pursuing a goal.

medical.title: We asked people with dementia about voluntary assisted dying. Here's what they said
medical.summary: What do Australians with dementia think about voluntary assisted dying? Until recently, no researchers had thought to ask.

medical.title: Number of older adults living with opioid use disorder in Ontario more than doubles over eight years, new report finds
medical.summary: The number of Ontarians aged 55 and older with health care interactions related to opioid use disorder (OUD) more than doubled between 2017 and 2025, according to a new report published by the Ontario Drug Policy Research Network (ODPRN), based at St. Michael's Hospital.

medical.title: Could quitting ultra-processed food boost mental health?
medical.summary: A preliminary study led by UC San Francisco adds to growing evidence that reducing ultra-processed food may improve symptoms of depression. Published in JAMA Psychiatry, the study is believed to be the first to compare symptoms in people with depression before and after they switched from their regular ultra-processed diet to healthier food.

medical.title: Newly discovered inflammatory cell signaling could open the door to autoimmune disease treatments
medical.summary: Our understanding of how cells interact with each other has been driven for decades by the central concept of receptor-mediated signal transduction. Now, researchers from Boston Children's Hospital are reporting the discovery of a new, receptor-free means of signal transduction.

medical.title: Year-old brain organoids reveal astrocytes may fuel early-onset epilepsy
medical.summary: Tiny, year-old human brain organoids that mimic the brain of a newborn are providing new clues to potential treatments for a leading genetic cause of childhood epilepsy that typically manifests as the brain matures shortly after birth.

medical.title: 'Dark genome' reveals different routes to inflammation in age-related condition
medical.summary: The study, published in GeroScience, investigated mutations in DNMT3A and TET2, the two most common mutations in clonal hematopoiesis, an age-related condition in which mutated blood stem cells expand and form larger populations of blood cells.

medical.title: A shorter, better-tolerated treatment for Chagas disease is possible
medical.summary: A 30-day course of benznidazole taken once a day could offer people with chronic Trypanosoma cruzi infection a safer and more practical option than the current standard treatment, taken twice a day for 60 days. The results of the TESEO trial, co-led by the Barcelona Institute for Global Health (ISGlobal), the University of Texas at El Paso (UTEP, U.S.), and CEADES (Bolivia), are published in The Lancet Infectious Diseases.

medical.title: Simple test could take the pain out of uterine cancer check
medical.summary: A new test using cells collected from urine and vaginal fluid could help rule out uterine and other cancers in most women who experience bleeding after menopause, University of Manchester researchers have found. Their study, published Sept. 22 in The Lancet Obstetrics, Gynaecology & Women's Health, found that the test could potentially reduce the need for invasive hospital tests, easing anxiety during what can be a distressing time for many women.

medical.title: PATHFINDER 2 findings advance multi-cancer early detection blood testing
medical.summary: A single blood draw that screens for more than 50 cancers substantially increased cancer detection when added to standard screening, identifying cancers that otherwise might have gone undetected until later stages, according to a new study from the Oregon Health & Science University Knight Cancer Institute.

medical.title: Could Earth's magnetic field influence how we age?
medical.summary: The Earth's magnetic field may influence how cells produce energy, physical performance and even lifespan, according to new research from the University of Nottingham.

medical.title: Think cannabis reduces stress? New study finds it's complicated
medical.summary: Cannabis is often used as a stress reliever, but a new study suggests that some of the body's stress response systems don't get the message.

science.title: Exercise keeps astronauts' hearts strong enough for flight to Mars
science.summary: Intense exercise during long spaceflights helps maintain heart structure and function within a range needed to tolerate the low-gravity environment of Mars, a study co-led by a UT Southwestern Medical Center researcher suggests. The findings, published in Circulation, not only address an issue critical to future space missions but could also lead to better interventions to improve heart health on Earth.

science.title: Variations in virus tails may help predict which phages kill more bacterial strains
science.summary: Bacteriophages—or phages, for short—are viruses that kill bacteria, and scientists have been studying them for decades as a possible solution to antibiotic-resistant infections. But phages are notoriously picky eaters—a phage that can eradicate one bacterial strain is often powerless against others, even if the bacteria are closely related. This means a phage that works for one patient may be useless for the next.

science.title: Facial recognition trial by police in Australia delivered strong results. But was it an ethical success?
science.summary: The results of Australia's first live facial recognition trial have been released. Since June 2026, the Western Australian Police Force has been testing the technology across metropolitan and regional WA.

science.title: Tic-tac-toe simulator offers a way to teach quantum physics without matrix algebra
science.summary: A team from SUNY Polytechnic Institute has designed a quantum rule-based simulator known as Quantum Tic-Tac-Toe. The simulator was originally designed to help students learn abstract concepts in quantum mechanics without using matrix algebra, in a game-like environment. It has rules similar to classical tic-tac-toe but incorporates phenomena from quantum mechanics, such as wavefunction collapse, quantum entanglement and quantum superposition. These concepts are also cornerstones of how quantum computers operate.

science.title: Roaming black holes may tell the hidden history of galaxies
science.summary: If you want to understand the origins of black holes, Yale astronomers say, you need to look beyond the centers of galaxies and start searching in the nooks and crannies. That's where you'll find the "wanderers"—black holes whose journeys may tell the story of how the first black holes formed.

science.title: New mining map highlights damage caused by extracting metals for your smartphone
science.summary: The most sustainable smartphone is the one you currently own. An estimated 80% of your phone's negative impact on the environment happens before the first minute of use—before it is even unboxed.

science.title: Bizarre new dinosaur with giant claws discovered in China
science.summary: It walked on two legs and may have looked like a feathered bear with giant claws. Meet Kayrasaurus changliensis—well, its almost complete skeleton, to be precise.

science.title: Spin waves inside a nano-oscillator imaged for the first time
science.summary: For the first time, researchers have directly imaged the magnetization dynamics inside a spin Hall nano-oscillator—a nanoscale device that converts direct current into tunable microwave signals and is a promising building block for energy-efficient wireless communication and brain-inspired computing.

science.title: SKA may detect magnetic fields on distant exoplanets
science.summary: Studying exoplanets has given astronomers insights into the characteristics that could help them find life beyond Earth. For years, astronomers thought an exoplanet's location in a star's habitable zone was enough to make it an Earth-like world. But some stars are more active than our sun, exposing planets in their habitable zones to far more radiation than Earth receives. Astronomers have increasingly recognized that a planet's magnetic field, which shields Earth from harmful radiation, could be a key characteristic in identifying Earth-like worlds.

science.title: DIY filter systems improve air quality in classrooms
science.summary: As students return to school and cold and flu season begins, researchers are studying ways to improve indoor air quality and reduce the risk of airborne disease transmission.

science.title: Report calls for government to introduce a charge on disposable cups
science.summary: Around 2.5 billion single-use cups are used in the U.K. every year, yet fewer than 1% are recycled. They contribute to litter, contaminate recycling streams and increase waste management and street cleaning costs for local authorities and taxpayers.

science.title: Why a healthy seafloor matters for the Earth system
science.summary: The seafloor is more than just the ground beneath the sea. Two-thirds of Earth's surface is covered by oceans, which have an average depth of almost 4 kilometers (2.5 miles). For a long time, the seafloor's remoteness protected it from widespread human disturbance. But that is changing: Bottom trawling now reaches depths of around 4,000 meters (13,100 feet) and already disturbs up to 2% of the global seafloor each year.

science.title: Hunting broadly not responsible for birds declining across Europe, study finds
science.summary: Hunting is not the main reason bird populations are declining across Europe, according to new research from University College Dublin in collaboration with the Spanish research institute Instituto de Investigación en Recursos Cinegéticos (IREC).

science.title: Adding limestone to Mississippi River Basin farmlands acts as a major carbon sink, study finds
science.summary: In a discovery as broad and far-reaching as the Big Muddy itself, a new Yale–led study says farmers in the Mississippi River Basin are storing more carbon dioxide (CO2) in the soil than they emit when they add limestone to their fields, an agricultural practice known as "liming."

science.title: How evolution shaped the human skeleton: Clues from cartilage
science.summary: Human and chimpanzee genomes are more than 98% identical, and the genes themselves barely differ. The changes that make us human are thought to hide instead in the DNA that controls when and where genes switch on.

science.title: Bat genomes and fossils point to a European origin 65 million years ago
science.summary: New research from the University of St Andrews has created the largest combined study of bat genomes and fossils ever undertaken, finding that bats most likely originated in Europe around 65 million years ago before spreading across the world.

science.title: Earth may have gained optimal conditions for life's chemistry 4.33 billion years ago
science.summary: Conditions on early Earth may have become stable enough to sustain the chemistry associated with the origins of life around 4.33 billion years ago, according to new research co-led by Planetary Science Institute senior scientist Oleg Abramov.

science.title: The dingo debate is heating up. How we manage these animals will determine their future
science.summary: What should we do about dingoes?

science.title: Buy, wear, return: Retail fraud and abuse explored in new study
science.summary: New research reveals retailers are losing money through two kinds of problematic returns: deliberate fraud and opportunistic abuse of generous return policies.

science.title: Seabed surveys around the Isles of Scilly find more than 90 species across habitats poorly captured by classifications
science.summary: Scientists have conducted an unprecedented assessment of the seabed around the Isles of Scilly, revealing complex mosaics of sediment that support a wide range of habitat-building species. The research, led by the University of Plymouth, used a range of techniques to monitor sediments around the archipelago and explore the diversity of species living within them.

science.title: Silicon solar cells could cut satellite power costs by up to 90%
science.summary: Switching to modern silicon solar cells could cut the cost of powering satellites by as much as 90% based on beginning-of-life (BOL) performance, according to a review led by the University of Surrey. The switch to silicon cells could also halve the weight of the solar cells needed on a spacecraft, freeing mass for fuel or instruments or cutting launch costs.

science.title: Why do politicians often want to change the school curriculum?
science.summary: Both sides of Australian politics are saying the school curriculum needs to change.

science.title: Quantum device simulates matter popping into existence
science.summary: A research team led by faculty at the Duke Quantum Center (DQC) has observed string-breaking dynamics related to particle-antiparticle formation on a quantum simulator, among the first such observations in quantum physics.

science.title: Could negative mass exist and be observed?
science.summary: Unlike electric charge, as far as we know all mass is positive, and positive masses attract one another. Could negative mass exist, and if so, what would be the ramifications?

science.title: Arts and culture key to inclusive climate action
science.summary: The arts, cultural and creative sectors can act as powerful catalysts for climate action, changing how people understand, engage with and act on climate change, new research from University College Cork (UCC) has found.

environment.summary: Indigenous land restitution in Chile came with a mixed bag of environmental outcomes and did not boost natural forest cover, according to a new study published in Nature Sustainability. While the return of ancestral lands gave the Indigenous Mapuche communities in southern Chile greater control over how their land was used — leading to an […]

environment.title: 1.4-million-year-old footprints reveal a surprisingly large human relative
environment.summary: Ancient footprints in Kenya reveal that eight Paranthropus boisei may have traveled together 1.4 million years ago, with some individuals reaching surprisingly large, human-like body sizes. The tracks offer a rare glimpse of their social behavior and suggest these extinct human relatives may have lived in more complex groups than previously thought.

environment.title: Seven new frog species were hiding beneath Madagascar’s forest floor
environment.summary: Scientists have discovered seven new species of Madagascar’s elusive diamond frogs, using DNA from modern and century-old museum specimens to solve a long-running biological puzzle. The findings reveal surprising hidden diversity and could help protect these little-known amphibians as their forest habitats disappear.

environment.title: Ancient Egyptian princesses were buried with weapons. Their bones reveal why
environment.summary: Weapons buried with ancient Egyptian princesses may have been more than ceremonial decorations. Researchers studying royal mummies from Dahshur found bone changes consistent with years of archery and other strenuous weapon use. Several women also showed evidence of healed injuries, suggesting surprisingly active lifestyles that may have included hunting or military training.

environment.title: A Manhattan-sized ice island just broke free from Greenland
environment.summary: A huge section of Greenland’s Petermann Glacier has snapped off, forming an ice island about the size of Manhattan. Satellites watched cracks spread rapidly before the 76-square-kilometer slab finally broke free on August 4. It is the glacier’s biggest calving event since 2012, and scientists say two even larger pieces could eventually follow. The rare Arctic iceberg will now be tracked as it drifts, breaks apart, and potentially affects shipping routes.

environment.title: Atomic catalyst unlocks the hidden value of plant waste
environment.summary: Scientists have created a highly efficient catalyst that breaks down stubborn lignin from plant waste into useful chemicals under relatively mild conditions. By revealing exactly how the catalyst works at the atomic level, the discovery could help turn forestry and agricultural waste into renewable building blocks for fuels, plastics, and other materials.

environment.title: Scientists find hidden “highways” guiding animal evolution
environment.summary: A sweeping analysis of thousands of animal genomes suggests that chromosomes do not evolve randomly but instead follow a limited number of irreversible “evolutionary highways.” These one-way genetic changes preserve clues to more than 600 million years of animal history and could even help researchers explore where evolution may head next.

environment.title: NASA finds Earth microbes could survive on the Moon
environment.summary: NASA scientists found that microbes brought by astronauts could survive in cold, shadowed niches around the Moon’s South Pole, potentially complicating future searches for pristine lunar chemistry. Some refuges may be no larger than a footprint, while one hardy fungus could even withstand limited exposure to sunlight.

mix_items.title: Exercise keeps astronauts' hearts strong enough for flight to Mars
mix_items.summary: Intense exercise during long spaceflights helps maintain heart structure and function within a range needed to tolerate the low-gravity environment of Mars, a study co-led by a UT Southwestern Medical Center researcher suggests. The findings, published in Circulation, not only address an issue critical to future space missions but could also lead to better interventions to improve heart health on Earth.

mix_items.title: Variations in virus tails may help predict which phages kill more bacterial strains
mix_items.summary: Bacteriophages—or phages, for short—are viruses that kill bacteria, and scientists have been studying them for decades as a possible solution to antibiotic-resistant infections. But phages are notoriously picky eaters—a phage that can eradicate one bacterial strain is often powerless against others, even if the bacteria are closely related. This means a phage that works for one patient may be useless for the next.

mix_items.summary: Substantially reduced intraoperative crystalloid fluid administration is not associated with worse patient-centered surgical outcomes, according to a study published online Sept. 15 in JAMA Network Open.

mix_items.title: Peptide may offer multipronged approach to neurodegenerative disease
mix_items.summary: Alzheimer's disease and related neurodegenerative disorders are among medicine's most challenging conditions, progressively impairing memory, movement and independence. Now, researchers at the University of California San Diego School of Medicine have identified a naturally occurring peptide—a small protein fragment called catestatin (CST)—that may help counter several key processes driving neurodegeneration.

mix_items.title: Same depression diagnosis, opposite brain patterns: Five profiles emerge
mix_items.summary: According to the World Health Organization, depression affects roughly 332 million (5.2%) adults globally. In Finland, depression is the most common single cause of both prolonged absences due to illness and disability pensions. Because two people with considerably different symptoms may receive the same depression diagnosis, researchers at the University of Helsinki wanted to determine whether this individuality also appears in brain activity.

mix_items.title: Tic-tac-toe simulator offers a way to teach quantum physics without matrix algebra
mix_items.summary: A team from SUNY Polytechnic Institute has designed a quantum rule-based simulator known as Quantum Tic-Tac-Toe. The simulator was originally designed to help students learn abstract concepts in quantum mechanics without using matrix algebra, in a game-like environment. It has rules similar to classical tic-tac-toe but incorporates phenomena from quantum mechanics, such as wavefunction collapse, quantum entanglement and quantum superposition. These concepts are also cornerstones of how quantum computers operate.

mix_items.title: Roaming black holes may tell the hidden history of galaxies
mix_items.summary: If you want to understand the origins of black holes, Yale astronomers say, you need to look beyond the centers of galaxies and start searching in the nooks and crannies. That's where you'll find the "wanderers"—black holes whose journeys may tell the story of how the first black holes formed.

mix_items.title: How a specific protein may drive brain damage in neuroHIV
mix_items.summary: While powerful medications can suppress the spread of HIV and its progression to AIDS, there are no cures, and many people living with HIV experience nervous system problems. Called neuroHIV, these complications occur when HIV infection affects the function and structural integrity of the brain and, to some extent, the spinal cord and peripheral nervous system.

mix_items.title: New mining map highlights damage caused by extracting metals for your smartphone
mix_items.summary: The most sustainable smartphone is the one you currently own. An estimated 80% of your phone's negative impact on the environment happens before the first minute of use—before it is even unboxed.

mix_items.title: Teen mental health problems rise, with sharper increase among girls than boys
mix_items.summary: In the first survey period (2007–2008), around 10% of girls were above the threshold for clinically significant mental health problems. In the second survey period (2024–2025), the corresponding figure was about 30%—approximately three times higher.

mix_items.title: What science says about ultraprocessed foods and the aging brain
mix_items.summary: The colorings, additives and preservatives added to food products, as well as food processing techniques, are a source of concern in 2026 because they are ubiquitous worldwide, yet their effects on metabolic health are not fully understood. Researchers are also increasingly investigating how they may affect the brain as people age. Dr. Owen Carmichael of LSU's Pennington Biomedical Research Center is helping advance that understanding through a comprehensive look at the potential relationship between ultraprocessed foods—those featuring extensive processing and additives—and the aging brain.

mix_items.title: Blood tests could identify early signs of cancer years before diagnosis
mix_items.summary: A study of blood samples collected up to nine years before a cancer diagnosis found changes in the DNA that captured the body's response to early traces of cancer development.

mix_items.title: Bizarre new dinosaur with giant claws discovered in China
mix_items.summary: It walked on two legs and may have looked like a feathered bear with giant claws. Meet Kayrasaurus changliensis—well, its almost complete skeleton, to be precise.

mix_items.title: Spin waves inside a nano-oscillator imaged for the first time
mix_items.summary: For the first time, researchers have directly imaged the magnetization dynamics inside a spin Hall nano-oscillator—a nanoscale device that converts direct current into tunable microwave signals and is a promising building block for energy-efficient wireless communication and brain-inspired computing.

mix_items.title: New filters help genetic sequencing flag possible causes of meningitis and encephalitis
mix_items.summary: New research led by Aston University's Dr. Ghaniah Hassan-Smith has found a new way to diagnose infections of the central nervous system, such as meningitis and encephalitis, that can be difficult to identify using conventional methods.

mix_items.title: Should you get a prostate-specific antigen test for prostate cancer?
mix_items.summary: Prostate cancer is common. About 200 in every 1,000 Australian men will be told they have prostate cancer by age 85. But the chance of dying from it is much lower: around 18 in 1,000 cases.

mix_items.title: SKA may detect magnetic fields on distant exoplanets
mix_items.summary: Studying exoplanets has given astronomers insights into the characteristics that could help them find life beyond Earth. For years, astronomers thought an exoplanet's location in a star's habitable zone was enough to make it an Earth-like world. But some stars are more active than our sun, exposing planets in their habitable zones to far more radiation than Earth receives. Astronomers have increasingly recognized that a planet's magnetic field, which shields Earth from harmful radiation, could be a key characteristic in identifying Earth-like worlds.

mix_items.title: Dementia caregiving can expose hidden family tensions—but early planning can ease the strain
mix_items.summary: "Families are messy, aren't they?" a daughter commented during a series of focus groups I ran with caregivers of older adults with memory issues.

mix_items.title: DIY filter systems improve air quality in classrooms
mix_items.summary: As students return to school and cold and flu season begins, researchers are studying ways to improve indoor air quality and reduce the risk of airborne disease transmission.

mix_items.title: Social media offers little substitute for real-life emotional support, research suggests
mix_items.summary: Two new papers by Oregon State University scientists suggest that social media may do little to replace the emotional support people receive from in-person relationships and that the timing of social media use may matter for a person's mental health.

mix_items.title: Report calls for government to introduce a charge on disposable cups
mix_items.summary: Around 2.5 billion single-use cups are used in the U.K. every year, yet fewer than 1% are recycled. They contribute to litter, contaminate recycling streams and increase waste management and street cleaning costs for local authorities and taxpayers.

mix_items.title: Why a healthy seafloor matters for the Earth system
mix_items.summary: The seafloor is more than just the ground beneath the sea. Two-thirds of Earth's surface is covered by oceans, which have an average depth of almost 4 kilometers (2.5 miles). For a long time, the seafloor's remoteness protected it from widespread human disturbance. But that is changing: Bottom trawling now reaches depths of around 4,000 meters (13,100 feet) and already disturbs up to 2% of the global seafloor each year.

mix_items.title: Turning scar-forming cells into neurons helps restore movement after spinal cord injury
mix_items.summary: What if cells that form scars after a spinal cord injury could become part of the repair process? Researchers have developed a genetic system that converts certain scar-forming cells into neurons, improving movement in mice and rats with spinal cord injuries.

mix_items.title: Fiber is both diet fad and fixture for good health—why there is no one‑size‑fits‑all way to increase intake
mix_items.summary: The numbers are clear: Americans aren't getting enough fiber.

mix_items.title: Hunting broadly not responsible for birds declining across Europe, study finds
mix_items.summary: Hunting is not the main reason bird populations are declining across Europe, according to new research from University College Dublin in collaboration with the Spanish research institute Instituto de Investigación en Recursos Cinegéticos (IREC).

mix_items.title: 'Frustration brake failure' hypothesis proposes new way to understand addiction
mix_items.summary: Why does a person continue seeking drugs when doing so becomes increasingly difficult, frustrating or harmful? Researchers at The University of Texas Medical Branch (UTMB) propose that part of the answer may involve a breakdown in a natural behavioral "brake" that normally signals when it is time to stop pursuing a goal.

mix_items.title: We asked people with dementia about voluntary assisted dying. Here's what they said
mix_items.summary: What do Australians with dementia think about voluntary assisted dying? Until recently, no researchers had thought to ask.

mix_items.title: Number of older adults living with opioid use disorder in Ontario more than doubles over eight years, new report finds
mix_items.summary: The number of Ontarians aged 55 and older with health care interactions related to opioid use disorder (OUD) more than doubled between 2017 and 2025, according to a new report published by the Ontario Drug Policy Research Network (ODPRN), based at St. Michael's Hospital.

mix_items.title: Adding limestone to Mississippi River Basin farmlands acts as a major carbon sink, study finds
mix_items.summary: In a discovery as broad and far-reaching as the Big Muddy itself, a new Yale–led study says farmers in the Mississippi River Basin are storing more carbon dioxide (CO2) in the soil than they emit when they add limestone to their fields, an agricultural practice known as "liming."

mix_items.title: Could quitting ultra-processed food boost mental health?
mix_items.summary: A preliminary study led by UC San Francisco adds to growing evidence that reducing ultra-processed food may improve symptoms of depression. Published in JAMA Psychiatry, the study is believed to be the first to compare symptoms in people with depression before and after they switched from their regular ultra-processed diet to healthier food.

mix_items.title: Newly discovered inflammatory cell signaling could open the door to autoimmune disease treatments
mix_items.summary: Our understanding of how cells interact with each other has been driven for decades by the central concept of receptor-mediated signal transduction. Now, researchers from Boston Children's Hospital are reporting the discovery of a new, receptor-free means of signal transduction.

mix_items.title: How evolution shaped the human skeleton: Clues from cartilage
mix_items.summary: Human and chimpanzee genomes are more than 98% identical, and the genes themselves barely differ. The changes that make us human are thought to hide instead in the DNA that controls when and where genes switch on.

mix_items.title: Year-old brain organoids reveal astrocytes may fuel early-onset epilepsy
mix_items.summary: Tiny, year-old human brain organoids that mimic the brain of a newborn are providing new clues to potential treatments for a leading genetic cause of childhood epilepsy that typically manifests as the brain matures shortly after birth.

mix_items.title: 'Dark genome' reveals different routes to inflammation in age-related condition
mix_items.summary: The study, published in GeroScience, investigated mutations in DNMT3A and TET2, the two most common mutations in clonal hematopoiesis, an age-related condition in which mutated blood stem cells expand and form larger populations of blood cells.

mix_items.title: Bat genomes and fossils point to a European origin 65 million years ago
mix_items.summary: New research from the University of St Andrews has created the largest combined study of bat genomes and fossils ever undertaken, finding that bats most likely originated in Europe around 65 million years ago before spreading across the world.

mix_items.title: Earth may have gained optimal conditions for life's chemistry 4.33 billion years ago
mix_items.summary: Conditions on early Earth may have become stable enough to sustain the chemistry associated with the origins of life around 4.33 billion years ago, according to new research co-led by Planetary Science Institute senior scientist Oleg Abramov.

mix_items.title: The dingo debate is heating up. How we manage these animals will determine their future
mix_items.summary: What should we do about dingoes?

mix_items.title: A shorter, better-tolerated treatment for Chagas disease is possible
mix_items.summary: A 30-day course of benznidazole taken once a day could offer people with chronic Trypanosoma cruzi infection a safer and more practical option than the current standard treatment, taken twice a day for 60 days. The results of the TESEO trial, co-led by the Barcelona Institute for Global Health (ISGlobal), the University of Texas at El Paso (UTEP, U.S.), and CEADES (Bolivia), are published in The Lancet Infectious Diseases.

mix_items.title: Simple test could take the pain out of uterine cancer check
mix_items.summary: A new test using cells collected from urine and vaginal fluid could help rule out uterine and other cancers in most women who experience bleeding after menopause, University of Manchester researchers have found. Their study, published Sept. 22 in The Lancet Obstetrics, Gynaecology & Women's Health, found that the test could potentially reduce the need for invasive hospital tests, easing anxiety during what can be a distressing time for many women.

mix_items.title: Buy, wear, return: Retail fraud and abuse explored in new study
mix_items.summary: New research reveals retailers are losing money through two kinds of problematic returns: deliberate fraud and opportunistic abuse of generous return policies.

mix_items.title: PATHFINDER 2 findings advance multi-cancer early detection blood testing
mix_items.summary: A single blood draw that screens for more than 50 cancers substantially increased cancer detection when added to standard screening, identifying cancers that otherwise might have gone undetected until later stages, according to a new study from the Oregon Health & Science University Knight Cancer Institute.

mix_items.title: Could Earth's magnetic field influence how we age?
mix_items.summary: The Earth's magnetic field may influence how cells produce energy, physical performance and even lifespan, according to new research from the University of Nottingham.

mix_items.title: Seabed surveys around the Isles of Scilly find more than 90 species across habitats poorly captured by classifications
mix_items.summary: Scientists have conducted an unprecedented assessment of the seabed around the Isles of Scilly, revealing complex mosaics of sediment that support a wide range of habitat-building species. The research, led by the University of Plymouth, used a range of techniques to monitor sediments around the archipelago and explore the diversity of species living within them.

mix_items.title: Think cannabis reduces stress? New study finds it's complicated
mix_items.summary: Cannabis is often used as a stress reliever, but a new study suggests that some of the body's stress response systems don't get the message.

mix_items.title: Silicon solar cells could cut satellite power costs by up to 90%
mix_items.summary: Switching to modern silicon solar cells could cut the cost of powering satellites by as much as 90% based on beginning-of-life (BOL) performance, according to a review led by the University of Surrey. The switch to silicon cells could also halve the weight of the solar cells needed on a spacecraft, freeing mass for fuel or instruments or cutting launch costs.

mix_items.title: Why do politicians often want to change the school curriculum?
mix_items.summary: Both sides of Australian politics are saying the school curriculum needs to change.

mix_items.title: Quantum device simulates matter popping into existence
mix_items.summary: A research team led by faculty at the Duke Quantum Center (DQC) has observed string-breaking dynamics related to particle-antiparticle formation on a quantum simulator, among the first such observations in quantum physics.

mix_items.title: Could negative mass exist and be observed?
mix_items.summary: Unlike electric charge, as far as we know all mass is positive, and positive masses attract one another. Could negative mass exist, and if so, what would be the ramifications?

mix_items.title: Arts and culture key to inclusive climate action
mix_items.summary: The arts, cultural and creative sectors can act as powerful catalysts for climate action, changing how people understand, engage with and act on climate change, new research from University College Cork (UCC) has found.

mix_items.title: Indigenous land back in Chile brings mixed bag of environmental outcomes: Study
mix_items.summary: Indigenous land restitution in Chile came with a mixed bag of environmental outcomes and did not boost natural forest cover, according to a new study published in Nature Sustainability. While the return of ancestral lands gave the Indigenous Mapuche communities in southern Chile greater control over how their land was used — leading to an […]

mix_items.title: 1.4-million-year-old footprints reveal a surprisingly large human relative
mix_items.summary: Ancient footprints in Kenya reveal that eight Paranthropus boisei may have traveled together 1.4 million years ago, with some individuals reaching surprisingly large, human-like body sizes. The tracks offer a rare glimpse of their social behavior and suggest these extinct human relatives may have lived in more complex groups than previously thought.

mix_items.title: Seven new frog species were hiding beneath Madagascar’s forest floor
mix_items.summary: Scientists have discovered seven new species of Madagascar’s elusive diamond frogs, using DNA from modern and century-old museum specimens to solve a long-running biological puzzle. The findings reveal surprising hidden diversity and could help protect these little-known amphibians as their forest habitats disappear.

mix_items.title: Ancient Egyptian princesses were buried with weapons. Their bones reveal why
mix_items.summary: Weapons buried with ancient Egyptian princesses may have been more than ceremonial decorations. Researchers studying royal mummies from Dahshur found bone changes consistent with years of archery and other strenuous weapon use. Several women also showed evidence of healed injuries, suggesting surprisingly active lifestyles that may have included hunting or military training.

mix_items.title: A Manhattan-sized ice island just broke free from Greenland
mix_items.summary: A huge section of Greenland’s Petermann Glacier has snapped off, forming an ice island about the size of Manhattan. Satellites watched cracks spread rapidly before the 76-square-kilometer slab finally broke free on August 4. It is the glacier’s biggest calving event since 2012, and scientists say two even larger pieces could eventually follow. The rare Arctic iceberg will now be tracked as it drifts, breaks apart, and potentially affects shipping routes.

mix_items.title: Atomic catalyst unlocks the hidden value of plant waste
mix_items.summary: Scientists have created a highly efficient catalyst that breaks down stubborn lignin from plant waste into useful chemicals under relatively mild conditions. By revealing exactly how the catalyst works at the atomic level, the discovery could help turn forestry and agricultural waste into renewable building blocks for fuels, plastics, and other materials.

mix_items.title: Scientists find hidden “highways” guiding animal evolution
mix_items.summary: A sweeping analysis of thousands of animal genomes suggests that chromosomes do not evolve randomly but instead follow a limited number of irreversible “evolutionary highways.” These one-way genetic changes preserve clues to more than 600 million years of animal history and could even help researchers explore where evolution may head next.

mix_items.title: NASA finds Earth microbes could survive on the Moon
mix_items.summary: NASA scientists found that microbes brought by astronauts could survive in cold, shadowed niches around the Moon’s South Pole, potentially complicating future searches for pristine lunar chemistry. Some refuges may be no larger than a footprint, while one hardy fungus could even withstand limited exposure to sunlight.
